Anthropic Just Posted $16.8 Billion in a Quarter and That Is Exactly Why People Are Nervous About an AI Bubble

The numbers coming out of the AI industry are the biggest in the history of technology, and a growing group of analysts thinks that is the problem. I went through the real figures behind the bubble debate, Anthropic’s revenue, the infrastructure commitments, the debt, the falling cost of intelligence, and who is actually paying, because the case for a correction and the case against it both rest on the same facts.

In the middle of October 2026, the Financial Times got hold of a number Anthropic had shared with potential investors at a private meeting, and it set off a week of nerves across the AI industry. The number was not bad. It was enormous. Anthropic told investors its revenue for the third quarter reached $16.8 billion, a figure Reuters and Bloomberg both matched soon after. For a company this young, that is close to unprecedented. The nervousness is not about the size of the number. It is about its shape, because the quarter before, the growth rate was far higher, and in the AI industry a merely gigantic number that is decelerating reads as a warning.

I want to walk through the actual figures on both sides of the bubble argument, because this is a case where the bulls and the bears are looking at the same data and drawing opposite conclusions, and the only way to think clearly about it is to see the numbers plainly.

The number that started the panic

Here is the sequence that has people talking. Per Reuters, Anthropic’s revenue went from roughly $4.7 billion in the first quarter of 2026 to about $11.6 billion in the second, then to $16.8 billion in the third. That is growth of around 147% from Q1 to Q2, then about 45% from Q2 to Q3. Both are extraordinary rates most companies would never see. The issue is the drop between them. A business the whole AI narrative leans on going from 147% to 45% quarterly growth, in a single step, is the kind of thing that makes a market built on the promise of endless acceleration start asking questions.

That is the core of the bear case, and it is a mathematical one. The analyst Alberto Romero put it cleanly in his writing on the subject, it only takes some finite amount of time to turn a proud exponential into a disappointing sigmoid, an S shaped curve that rises fast and then flattens. Every exponential eventually hits a binding constraint and bends over. The question for Anthropic is whether what we just saw is noise in a still steep curve or the first visible bend.

The counterpoint is just as real. Reuters reported that investors who attended the meeting actually came away upbeat about the growth and the path to profit, and Anthropic told them the quarter was cash flow positive, a milestone most frontier AI labs have not reached. A deceleration from a once in history growth rate is not the same as a collapse. Both things are true at once, and which one matters more is exactly what the market is trying to price.

The valuation that has to come true

The reason the growth rate matters so much is the price tag attached to it. Bloomberg reported that some prospective investors see a fair valuation for Anthropic in the range of $1.8 trillion to $2 trillion ahead of a possible IPO. To grow into a number like that, the company cannot just stay huge, it has to keep compounding at rates that only make sense if AI revenue keeps expanding into enormous new markets. Anthropic recorded an operating loss of more than $8 billion in 2025 on revenue of roughly $4.6 billion, which is normal for a lab spending to reach the frontier, and it is also a lot of ground to make up. A valuation near $2 trillion is a bet that the compounding does not stop.

The money being spent is the part that cannot be undone

Set the revenue aside and look at the spending, because that is where the risk gets concrete. Building AI means building data centers, and data centers cost real money on fixed timelines whether or not the customers show up. A data center that costs $10 billion still costs $10 billion if the AI payoff arrives a decade late. The construction workers, the energy companies, the landowners, and the lenders all want dollars, not tokens, and they want them on schedule.

The lenders are where the strain is showing first. Take CoreWeave, a company that rents out GPUs to AI firms after pivoting from crypto mining. It has taken on roughly $52 billion in debt obligations, and in mid October 2026 the bond market turned on it. Its 2032 notes hit a 15% yield intraday on 13 October, and the stock fell as much as 16% the next day. A 15% yield is what investors demand to hold debt they consider risky, and this is for a company at the center of the supposedly most promising industry in history. Its interest bill, around $640 million in the second quarter alone, now runs ahead of its adjusted operating income. CoreWeave is an extreme case, but it is not an isolated one.

The pressure reaches the giants too. Oracle raised $43 billion in debt in a recent fiscal year and ended with negative free cash flow. Even Alphabet, one of the most stable companies on earth, generated about $39 billion in cash from operations in a single quarter and spent about $45 billion on infrastructure, turning its free cash flow negative for the first time since it went public in 2004. When Google has to borrow to keep building, the scale of the commitment is clear.

The gap between what is being spent and what is coming back

The single clearest way to frame the bubble question comes from Sequoia’s David Cahn, who has been tracking it since 2023. He started by asking how much revenue the industry needed to justify its infrastructure spending, and called it AI’s $200 billion question. By 2026 his updated math puts AI infrastructure spending for the year at about $1.5 trillion, and the revenue the industry would need to earn to justify those chips and data centers at around $3 trillion, a figure he thinks is probably an underestimate. Set that against where the industry actually is, and the distance is the whole argument.

Gartner put a number on the downside. It estimated that more than $3.5 trillion in AI infrastructure spending could face impairment by 2030, meaning written down as worth less than what was paid for it, if the current investment pace holds. The firm also projected that data centers will generate trillions of dollars less in revenue by 2030 than they would need to justify their cost and deliver expected returns. These are forecasts, not facts, and forecasts about 2030 are easy to wave away. The bear case is that markets do not wait for 2030. If investors become convinced today that the returns will not arrive on time, they sell today.

The cost of intelligence is falling off a cliff

Here is the figure I find hardest to argue with, and it cuts against every AI company at once. Per Epoch AI, the cost of achieving a fixed level of AI performance has been falling about 47% every quarter since 2023. That works out to roughly a thirteenfold reduction every year. The capability you spent billions to build this year gets dramatically cheaper for someone else to reproduce next year.

That is wonderful for anyone using AI and hard for anyone selling it at a premium. Google’s models improve, Meta has caught up from behind, Chinese labs ship capable models at low prices, and open weight alternatives handle the ordinary tasks for free. OpenAI sits toe to toe with Anthropic in the same markets, code, agents, and enterprise. When the thing you sell gets 13 times cheaper to make every year and several well funded competitors sell something similar, holding a premium price is genuinely difficult. The bull reply is Jevons paradox, that cheaper intelligence drives so much more usage that total revenue grows anyway. That can be true, and rising usage still does not guarantee rising profit when competition is this fierce and the product is drifting toward a commodity.

Almost nobody is actually paying yet

For all the money moving, the customer base is thinner than the valuations imply. Andreessen Horowitz, in its State of Markets report, found that only about 2% of US households were paying for any AI service as of April 2026. After this much progress and this much capability, 2% is a strikingly small share. On the enterprise side the picture is broad but shallow, nearly 30% of S&P 500 companies reported some AI impact, while only about 2% reported a tracked, quantifiable metric. Adoption is wide and usage is light.

There are early signs of belt tightening too. Reporting on Anthropic’s own customers suggests some of its largest corporate accounts have trimmed their spending as they build their own tools, and a few companies have capped what employees can spend on AI each month. None of this is fatal on its own. It does complicate the story that enterprise demand is an unstoppable escalator.

What a bubble actually means

A bubble is one of the most misunderstood words in this debate, so it is worth being precise about what it means. A bubble does not mean the technology is fake, or that every company goes bust, or that AI fails to change the world. It means the core premise behind the industry’s valuations has been inflated beyond what reality can support in the expected timeframe. The internet was real and world changing, and the dot com bubble still popped, because the prices had run ahead of the business. A bubble is a correction mechanism, not a verdict on the technology.

That distinction is why smart people land on opposite sides. You can believe AI is the most important technology of the century and also believe its current valuations are too high, those are not contradictory positions. The companies are, by most measures of product and growth, among the best startups ever built. The argument is about price and timing, not about whether the tools work.

Why the whole market is watching 1 company

The reason this is not a niche tech story is that the stock market has become unusually concentrated on AI. Reuters noted that the S&P 500 rose about 14% in a recent stretch even though more than 40% of its stocks were down, meaning a handful of large AI linked names carried the whole index. The Kobeissi Letter pointed out that the correlation between the equal weighted S&P 500 and the standard index had fallen to its lowest level on record, lower than during COVID and lower than the dot com peak. A market held up by a few names is a market with a thin margin for disappointment.

That is what ties Anthropic’s revenue growth to your retirement account. The financial engineering underneath is getting elaborate too. A UBS analysis described deals where investors buy chips from Google, lease them to Anthropic, and Google backstops parts of the arrangement, so several companies’ financial health depends on the same stream of future AI revenue showing up. There is nothing inherently wrong with structuring deals that way, and it does mean a shortfall in one place can ripple through many balance sheets at once.

What would actually settle it

Both sides agree on the test, they just disagree on the result. It comes down to whether run rate revenue, the annualized version of a recent strong month or quarter, turns into durable actual revenue, people and companies paying enough, for long enough, to justify the spending. If Anthropic reaccelerates in the fourth quarter, reaches its run rate targets, and enterprise adoption deepens, the bears will have been early and wrong. If growth keeps flattening while the infrastructure bills come due on schedule, the case for a correction gets stronger each quarter.

I do not know which way it breaks, and anyone who tells you they do with certainty is selling something. What I can say is that the numbers to watch are specific and public. Watch Anthropic’s next quarter for whether growth stabilizes or keeps sliding. Watch the bond yields at companies like CoreWeave for whether lenders calm down or tighten further. Watch the share of households and enterprises actually paying, not just experimenting. Those figures, not the rhetoric, are where this gets decided.

Sources and further reading

  • Anthropic tells investors Q3 revenue reached $16.8bn, The Next Web
  • Anthropic revenue rises to $16.8 billion as IPO approaches but growth slows, Yahoo Finance
  • Can AI answer the $3 trillion question, David Cahn, TechCrunch
  • Gartner warns $3.5 trillion in AI infrastructure spending could face impairment by 2030, Crypto Briefing
  • CoreWeave shares plunge as bond yields near 15%, Crypto Briefing
  • The price of intelligence is falling rapidly, Epoch AI via Marginal Revolution
  • Only about 2% of US households pay for AI services, a16z finds, Crypto Briefing

Kubernetes CrashLoopBackOff: A Practical Troubleshooting Guide

If you have worked with Kubernetes, you may have encountered a pod that starts, fails, restarts, and repeats the same cycle.

Eventually, Kubernetes reports:

CrashLoopBackOff

The first instinct is often to restart the pod or redeploy the application. However, restarting a pod does not fix the underlying problem if the application continues to fail.

In this guide, we'll walk through a systematic way to investigate the issue, identify common causes, and choose the appropriate fix.

What does CrashLoopBackOff mean?

CrashLoopBackOff means a container in a pod has repeatedly terminated, and Kubernetes is delaying subsequent restart attempts.

It is a status indicating a restart problem, not the root cause itself.

The underlying issue could be an application crash, incorrect configuration, a missing dependency, a failed health check, or insufficient memory.

Step 1: Identify the affected pod

Start by listing pods in the namespace where your application runs:

kubectl get pods -n <namespace>

Example output:

NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS api-service-7d9f8c9b-x2k4p 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 5

Record the pod name and its restart count.

If you don't know the namespace, you can list pods across namespaces:

kubectl get pods -A

Step 2: Inspect the pod events

Next, examine the pod's configuration, container states, and recent events:

kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>

Pay attention to:

The container's last termination state.

The exit code and termination reason.

Liveness and readiness probe failures.

Events mentioning failed mounts, image problems, or resource limits.

For example, a termination reason of OOMKilled suggests the container was terminated after exceeding its memory limit.

Don't assume every CrashLoopBackOff is a memory issue. Use the evidence from the pod description to narrow the investigation.

Step 3: Read the previous container logs

This is one of the most useful troubleshooting commands:

kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace> --previous

The --previous flag requests logs from the previous terminated container instance, when available.

Look for messages such as:

Missing environment variables.

Database connection failures.

Invalid application configuration.

Permission errors.

Unhandled exceptions during startup.

If the container has not restarted yet, inspect its current logs instead:

kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace>

If the pod has multiple containers, specify the container name using -c <container-name>.

Step 4: Check the termination reason

Use the pod description and logs together to determine what happened.

Here are common scenarios:

FindingWhat to investigateOOMKilledMemory limit, memory usage, and possible leaksExit code 1Application errors and startup configurationExit code 137Forced termination; check whether memory pressure or another cause explains itLiveness probe failedProbe path, port, timing, and application healthMissing configurationEnvironment variables, ConfigMaps, and SecretsConnection refusedService availability, endpoint, port, and network configuration

An exit code alone is not always sufficient to identify the cause. Correlate it with events, logs, and the container's termination reason.

Step 5: Investigate health checks

A liveness probe tells Kubernetes whether a container should be restarted. A readiness probe determines whether it should receive normal service traffic.

A misconfigured liveness probe can restart an application that needs more time to initialize.

For example, consider this illustrative probe configuration:

livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /health port: 8080 initialDelaySeconds: 5 periodSeconds: 10

Before using this configuration, confirm that your application actually exposes /health on port 8080.

Also consider whether five seconds is enough for your application to start. If startup takes longer, review the probe timing and whether a startup probe is more appropriate.

Do not simply increase every timeout. First determine whether the application is genuinely unhealthy or the probe is incorrectly configured.

Step 6: Apply a targeted fix

Once you have identified the likely cause, make a change that addresses it.

Examples:

Application crash: Fix the exception or startup command.

Memory exhaustion: Investigate memory consumption and set appropriate resource requests and limits.

Configuration error: Correct the environment variable or configuration source.

Probe failure: Correct the endpoint, port, or timing.

Dependency unavailable: Check dependency health, connection settings, and retry behavior.

Avoid changing multiple unrelated settings simultaneously. Making one evidence-based change at a time makes it easier to determine whether the fix worked.

Step 7: Verify the result

After applying the fix through your normal deployment workflow, check the pod again:

kubectl get pods -n <namespace>

Then inspect the recent events and logs to confirm that the application starts successfully.

A pod showing Running is encouraging, but it is not the only success criterion. Check that the container remains healthy, readiness succeeds, and the application performs its intended function.

A simple troubleshooting workflow

When investigating CrashLoopBackOff, follow this order:

Identify the affected pod.

Run kubectl describe pod.

Inspect the previous container logs.

Check the termination reason and recent events.

Investigate the most likely root cause.

Apply a targeted fix.

Verify application health after the change.

This process helps avoid random restarts and unnecessary configuration changes.

Final thoughts

Kubernetes troubleshooting becomes easier when you distinguish the symptom from the root cause.

CrashLoopBackOff tells you that repeated restarts are happening. Your task is to discover why.

Start with the evidence, investigate one likely cause at a time, and verify the outcome after making a change.

References

Kubernetes: Debugging Pods

Kubernetes: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

medium.conteudo_html:
In this article, I would like to write about a bug in Wikinewsie and how I tackled it.

Here are a few quick things to know.

Wikinewsie is a web app that shows the most-edited Wikipedia.org articles over recent hours, automatically identifying current event topics and news that are undergoing active collaboration.

Wikimedia keeps its bug list on a website called Phabricator. Every bug gets a number starting with the letter T. Ours is T439940.

Here is the Open-source loop: Find a bug, make a branch, change the code, test it, save it, send it for review.

Fix untranslated labels in Wikinewsie after switching language: A Step-by-Step Walkthrough

The Bug Report:

Steps to replicate the issue (include links if applicable):

Open https://wikinewsie.toolforge.org/en
Use the language selector to pick another language (e.g., Polish)
What happens?:
Most of the elements are translated, but several are not.
In the Feed section -
*"Mix"
*"Editors"
*"Edits"

In the Mix weights section -

*"Edits"
*"Editors"
*"Growth"
*"Category"
*"New page"

What should have happened instead?:

These elements should have been shown in the newly selected language, instead of retaining the language of the initial selection.
Note that the bug doesn't appear when Polish interface is loaded directly, only when English is loaded first and then the language selector is used to switch to Polish.
Software version (on Special:Version page; skip for WMF-hosted wikis like Wikipedia):

Explaination:
On the Wikinewsie site, when someone opens the English version first and then uses the language dropdown to switch to Polish, most of the page changes to Polish, but a few words stay in English. Those words are:

  • In the Feed section: “Mix”, “Editors”, “Edits”
  • In the Mix weights section: “Edits”, “Editors”, “Growth”, “Category”, “New page”

Why does the bug matter? Think of a Polish reader. They pick Polish from the language dropdown and expect everything on the page in Polish. If a few buttons still say “Mix”, “Editors” and “Edits” in English, the page feels half-finished and confusing.

The plan

1. Make a new branch, so our work stays separate from the main code.
2. Find where the translations are stored.
3. Find which translation key belongs to each stuck label.
4. Find where the code uses those keys.
5. Work out why they do not update.
6. Fix it
7. Test it
8. Check that we changed only what we meant to change.
9. Commit, push, and open a merge request.

Switch to a new branch

git checkout -b fix-untranslated-labels-on-language-switch

Find where the translations are stored

Why we need it? Before fixing anything, we need to know where the words come from. We searched the whole project for one of the stuck labels.

grep -rni "mix weights" i18n src

What did we get?

./i18n/en.json:90:      "wikinewsie-mix-weights-label": "Mix weights:",

We learned two things from this:

1. The `i18n` folder holds the translations. (“i18n” is short for “internationalization”, which just means “making the app work in many languages”).

2. Think of it like a dictionary. The code asks for the key wikinewsie-mix-weights-label, and the language file hands back the right words Mix weights.

Find which translation key belongs to each stuck label.

We open the file i18/en.json and copy all the keys for the missing labels.

"wikinewsie-mix": "Mix",
"wikinewsie-edits": "Edits",
"wikinewsie-editors": "Editors",
"wikinewsie-growth": "Growth",
"wikinewsie-category": "Category",
"wikinewsie-new-page": "New page",

All six keys exist in the translation files. This confirms what the report hinted at: the translations are fine, so the problem must be in how the code uses them.

Find where the code uses these keys

We searched the `src` folder (where the app’s code lives) for the “Mix” key.

grep -rn "wikinewsie-mix'" src

The quote after the key makes it match wikinewsie-mix exactly, and not longer keys such as wikinewsie-mix-score

We found the culprit in src/App.vue :

const MODE_OPTIONS: Array<{ value: FeedMode; label: string; tooltip: string }> = [
  { value: 'score', label: text('wikinewsie-mix'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-mix-tooltip') },
  { value: 'editors', label: text('wikinewsie-editors'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-editors-tooltip') },
  { value: 'edits', label: text('wikinewsie-edits'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-edits-tooltip') },
];

Here is what each piece in that code is.

  • text('wikinewsie-mix') is the function that looks up a key and returns the words in the current language.
  • MODE_OPTIONS is the list of buttons for the Feed section.

Now the important part: when does text(…)run?

It runs once, at the moment the file loads and the list is created. At that moment the language is English, so the label is locked in as the plain word “Mix”. Later, when the user switches to Polish, the language changes, but this list is already built. Nobody rebuilds it. It keeps saying “Mix”.

It is like printing a menu. If you print it in English and the customer later asks for Polish, the printed menu does not change by itself. You have to print a new one.

Solution
Vue (the framework this app uses) has something called `computed` because of this Vue re-runs the whenever something it depends on changes.

We make the change to MODE_OPTIONS by adding computed

const MODE_OPTIONS = computed<Array<{ value: FeedMode; label: string; tooltip: string }>>(() => [
  { value: 'score', label: text('wikinewsie-mix'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-mix-tooltip') },
  { value: 'editors', label: text('wikinewsie-editors'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-editors-tooltip') },
  { value: 'edits', label: text('wikinewsie-edits'), tooltip: text('wikinewsie-edits-tooltip') },
]);

What changed:

  • The list is wrapped in computed(() => [...])

So far, we have got MODE_OPTIONS labels (Mix, Editors, Edits) covered now.

We go on to the next labels for WEIGHTS(Edits, Editors, Growth, Category, New page)

We begin by searching for the keys that only this list uses

grep -n "wikinewsie-growth\|wikinewsie-category\|wikinewsie-new-page" src/App.vue

That led us to WEIGHTS_FIELDS. We checked where it is used and just as the previous one, we have to add computed

BEFORE:

const WEIGHT_FIELDS: Array<{ key: keyof ScoreWeights; label: string }> = [
  { key: 'edits', label: text('wikinewsie-edits') },
  { key: 'editors', label: text('wikinewsie-editors') },
  { key: 'growth', label: text('wikinewsie-growth') },
  { key: 'category', label: text('wikinewsie-category') },
  { key: 'isNew', label: text('wikinewsie-new-page') },
];

AFTER:

const WEIGHT_FIELDS = computed<Array<{ key: keyof ScoreWeights; label: string }>>(() => [
  { key: 'edits', label: text('wikinewsie-edits') },
  { key: 'editors', label: text('wikinewsie-editors') },
  { key: 'growth', label: text('wikinewsie-growth') },
  { key: 'category', label: text('wikinewsie-category') },
  { key: 'isNew', label: text('wikinewsie-new-page') },
]);
  • The list is now wrapped in computed(() => [...])

We saved the file, switched English to Polish in the running app, and both the Feed buttons and Weights buttons changed immediately to Polish.

Save the changes and Push

git add src/App.vue
git commit -m "Fix untranslated labels after switching language"
git push -u origin fix-untranslated-labels-on-language-switch

Every Page of Your SPA Deserves a Preview: SEO for Vue and React Without Nuxt or Next.js

You share a product page on WhatsApp. Instead of the product image and name, the preview displays your website’s generic title. Sometimes, nothing appears at all. You try sharing another link from the same website and get the same result.

Google is not much better. Your pages appear with identical titles and descriptions, even though each page contains different content.

If you build applications with Vue or React, you have probably encountered this problem. Your application works perfectly in the browser, but search engines and social media platforms struggle to understand what each page is about.

I spent four years looking for a practical solution to this problem. Eventually, I built one.

Why This Happens

Most Vue and React single-page applications (SPAs) follow the same approach. The server sends a basic HTML document, and JavaScript renders the actual content in the browser.

Consider a typical HTML response:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>My Application</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Welcome to my application">
</head>
<body>
  <div id="app"></div>
  <script src="/assets/app.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

The browser loads the JavaScript bundle, and Vue or React renders the appropriate page. When users navigate to different routes, the application updates the content without requesting an entirely new HTML document.

This is excellent for building interactive applications. However, it creates a problem for social media crawlers and can complicate search engine optimization.

When someone shares a product URL on WhatsApp, Facebook, LinkedIn, or another platform, the platform’s crawler typically requests the URL and inspects the HTML response. It looks for metadata such as the page title, description, preview image, and canonical URL.

If every route returns the same HTML metadata, every shared link can produce the same preview.

Search engines can execute JavaScript in some circumstances, but relying on client-side rendering alone does not provide the same level of control as delivering the appropriate metadata in the initial HTML response.

Four Years of Searching for a Solution

For years, the usual recommendations have been Nuxt for Vue or Next.js for React. Both frameworks offer powerful server-side rendering (SSR) and static site generation (SSG) capabilities.

But what if your application is already built with Vue or React? What if your backend is already running on Laravel, Express, or another framework? What if you simply want each page to have the correct metadata without rebuilding your entire application?

Migrating to another framework is not always a realistic option.

Sometimes, you need a smaller, more targeted solution that fits into your existing architecture.

[Add one or two sentences describing the project where you first encountered this problem.]

I wanted a solution that would work with an existing SPA, generate page-specific metadata on the server, and leave the application’s frontend architecture untouched.

The Breakthrough: You Only Need the <head>

The key insight was simple: you do not necessarily need to render the entire page on the server to deliver the correct metadata.

For social media previews and many metadata-related SEO requirements, the important part is the HTML <head> section.

For example, a product page could return the following metadata:

<head>
  <title>Wireless Headphones | My Store</title>
  <meta
    name="description"
    content="Discover our wireless headphones with premium sound."
  >
  <meta
    property="og:title"
    content="Wireless Headphones | My Store"
  >
  <meta

The browser can still load the SPA and render the page as usual. The difference is that crawlers receive the correct metadata directly in the HTML response.

This approach does not replace full SSR or SSG. It addresses a more specific problem: delivering page-specific metadata without requiring a complete rendering framework.

Meet spa-meta-tags

I built spa-meta-tags, an open-source package designed to inject dynamic metadata into the HTML responses of existing single-page applications.

The idea is to keep your current architecture while making your pages more suitable for search engines and social media previews.

Installation

npm install spa-meta-tags

Basic example with Express

The package can be integrated into an existing Express server. You provide the metadata for the requested page, and the middleware injects it into your HTML response.

A simplified integration looks like this:

const express = require('express');
const { SpaMetaTags } = require('spa-meta-tags');
const app = express();
const spaMetaTags = new SpaMetaTags({
  // Configure the package according to your application.
});
// Register the metadata middleware before the SPA fallback.
app.use(async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    // Resolve metadata for the requested URL.
    // Apply it to the HTML response using spa-meta-tags.
    next();
  } catch (error) {
    next(error);
  }
});
// Serve your SPA's static files and fallback route here.

Consult the official documentation for the exact configuration options and complete working examples.

The important architectural principle is that the metadata must be resolved for the requested URL before the HTML response is sent. Your SPA can then continue operating as before.

What Changes for SEO?

With page-specific metadata delivered in the initial HTML response, you can provide different information for different routes.

1. Unique titles and descriptions

Each product, article, category, or landing page can have its own title and description.

This helps search engines understand the purpose of each page and gives users more relevant information in search results when that metadata is used.

2. Better social media previews

Open Graph metadata allows supported platforms to display the appropriate title, description, and image when a link is shared.

Instead of showing the same generic preview for every URL, your application can provide information that matches the actual page.

3. Canonical URLs

You can define the canonical URL for each page to indicate its preferred address to search engines.

This is useful when the same content can be accessed through multiple URLs.

4. Route-specific metadata and status handling

Different routes can return different metadata, including information appropriate for unavailable pages.

However, metadata alone does not make a nonexistent page a genuine HTTP 404 response. The server must also return the correct HTTP status code when a resource does not exist.

An important distinction

spa-meta-tags focuses on the HTML <head>. It does not automatically render the visible content of your application on the server.

If your goal is to make the entire page content available in the initial HTML response, or if you need broader SSR capabilities, Nuxt, Next.js, or another SSR/SSG solution may be more appropriate.

The purpose of spa-meta-tags is different: it provides a focused solution for metadata without forcing you to migrate your application.

Beyond SEO: Multi-Tenant Applications

While working on this solution, I also considered another use case: multi-tenant applications.

Imagine a platform where several companies have their own storefronts, subdomains, or custom domains. Each tenant needs its own metadata, branding, and potentially its own domain verification tags.

For example:

<meta
  name="facebook-domain-verification"
  content="TENANT_SPECIFIC_VERIFICATION_CODE"
>
<meta
  name="google-site-verification"
  content="TENANT_SPECIFIC_VERIFICATION_CODE"
>

These values may differ from one tenant to another.

By resolving the appropriate configuration on the server, you can return the correct metadata for the domain or tenant associated with the incoming request.

This makes the approach useful beyond traditional SEO, especially for SaaS platforms, marketplaces, and multi-tenant applications.

The same principle can also be extended to scripts that need to be present in the initial HTML response.

For example, some applications need to configure analytics or tracking tools such as Google Tag Manager, Facebook Pixel, or TikTok Pixel.

In a multi-tenant platform, the configuration may differ between tenants. Handling this at the server level can help ensure that the appropriate configuration is included in the HTML response.

Technical Decisions Behind the Package

Building a small package that fits into existing applications requires careful decisions. Here are some of the principles behind the project.

Zero dependencies

Keeping the dependency footprint small reduces installation overhead and avoids introducing unnecessary packages into an existing application.

Flexible integration

The goal is to integrate with an existing server rather than force developers to replace their frontend framework or rewrite their application.

Graceful failure

Metadata generation should not become a reason for an application to stop responding. When an external API or metadata source is unavailable, the server should be able to fall back to a safe response.

The package’s exact timeout and fallback behavior should be verified against the published version before documenting specific limits.

Safe HTML injection

Metadata values must be handled carefully before being inserted into HTML. Escaping values appropriately helps prevent malformed markup and injection vulnerabilities.

Caching

When metadata is expensive to retrieve or generate, caching can reduce repeated work. The caching strategy must account for differences between routes and tenants to avoid returning one page’s metadata for another.

Support for different deployment environments

Not every application runs on a dedicated Node.js server. Some projects are deployed to platforms such as Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, or GitHub Pages, while others use traditional shared hosting.

The appropriate implementation depends on the deployment environment. A server-side middleware solution requires a server or compatible runtime. Static hosting generally needs metadata to be generated during the build process or handled through another supported mechanism.

Check the documentation for the deployment modes actually supported by spa-meta-tags.

How to Get Started

If you already have a Vue or React SPA and want to improve its page metadata without migrating to Nuxt or Next.js, start by exploring the project.

  • Documentation: roazagba.github.io/spa-meta-tags
  • GitHub repository: github.com/roazagba/spa-meta-tags
  • npm package: npmjs.com/package/spa-meta-tags

Review the installation instructions and examples to determine whether the package fits your current architecture.

Final Thoughts

Single-page applications offer a great developer experience, but page-specific metadata can become a challenge when the initial HTML response is identical across routes.

Nuxt and Next.js provide comprehensive solutions through SSR and SSG. However, migrating an existing application is not always necessary or practical when the immediate requirement is to deliver the correct metadata.

That is the problem spa-meta-tags aims to solve.

The broader lesson is that you do not always need to replace your entire architecture to address a specific technical limitation. Sometimes, a small, carefully designed addition is enough to make an existing application work better.

If you build Vue or React applications, I would be interested to hear how you currently handle SEO and social media previews in your projects.

corrida_no_ar.titulo: KIPRUN lança TÊNIS COM SENSOR que avisa a troca. PRECISAMOS DISSO?
corrida_no_ar.resumo: O novo tênis da Kiprun que avisa a hora da troca, a correção sobre a elite da Meia de Valência, o calendário do Mountain Do 2027 e as novidades da Maratona da Bahia. E ainda: dados da 100ª Comrades, kits da Maratona de Pernambuco e a bela medalha de Nápoles.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Quinta-feira | 22 de outubro de 2026

A Kiprun, marca de corrida da Decathlon, apresentou o Kipnext Connect, um tênis equipado com um sensor que monitora o desgaste do amortecimento e informa o momento ideal para a troca do calçado. A novidade conquistou o primeiro lugar no “Decathlon Innovation Awards 2026”, uma premiação interna que reconhece os melhores projetos da companhia.

O principal diferencial é o sensor SOLL, de apenas três gramas e sem necessidade de bateria, que foi criado em parceria com a startup Mouvmenta. Ele acompanha a compressão da espuma de amortecimento durante o uso, e as informações são consultadas pelo corredor através do aplicativo “Kiprun Pacer”. A tecnologia busca oferecer uma avaliação individualizada, considerando fatores como peso, frequência de treinos e características da corrida, que influenciam na durabilidade do tênis. O projeto levou três anos para ser desenvolvido, com cerca de 300 protótipos e mais de 12 mil quilômetros de testes. Com preço anunciado de €219,99, o Kipnext Connect tem lançamento previsto para o fim de 2026.

Correção sobre a Meia Maratona de Valência

Uma correção importante: no programa de ontem, foi informado que Kenenisa Bekele correria a Maratona de Valência, mas na verdade ele participará da Meia Maratona de Valência. O field masculino da prova está forte, com sete atletas com tempos abaixo de 60 minutos. Surpreendentemente, Bekele não é um deles, com seu recorde pessoal de 1:00:22.

O campo feminino também está excelente, liderado pela ex-recordista mundial Yalemzerf Yehualaw, que tem 1:03:51. A prova contará com duas atletas abaixo de 1h05min e seis abaixo de 1h06min.

Calendário 2027 do Mountain Do

Para quem busca uma experiência de corrida completa, com medalhas e kits de alta qualidade, o circuito Mountain Do é uma ótima pedida. A organização divulgou o calendário para 2027, com etapas em locais incríveis:

  • Colônia de Sacramento, Uruguai
  • Praia do Rosa, Santa Catarina
  • Deserto da Namíbia, África
  • Chapada dos Veadeiros, Goiás
  • Costão do Santinho, Santa Catarina
  • Fim do Mundo, Ushuaia (Argentina)
  • Selva Amazônica, Amapá
  • Deserto do Sahara, Marrocos
  • Pantanal, Mato Grosso do Sul

Maratona da Bahia revela percurso e medalha

A Maratona da Bahia, que teve seu lançamento recente, divulgou a medalha e o percurso da prova. A medalha, assinada pelo renomado artista plástico Bel Borba, é uma verdadeira obra de arte, com um design diferenciado para a maratona e para as outras distâncias.

O percurso de 42 km largará do Mercado Modelo, passará ao lado da Arena Fonte Nova, contornará o Dique do Tororó, seguirá pela orla até o Farol da Barra e fará o retorno na Praça Osório Vilas-Boas, voltando para a chegada no Mercado Modelo. A altimetria acumulada será de 218 metros de ganho, um percurso razoável para uma maratona.

Estatísticas da 100ª Comrades Marathon

A 100ª edição da Comrades Marathon promete ser grandiosa. As inscrições foram um sucesso, com 56.283 solicitações para um total de 28.070 vagas aceitas. A prova reunirá atletas de 129 países e territórios. As mulheres representarão 29,6% dos participantes, um número crescente. A faixa etária com mais inscritos é a de 40 a 49 anos, e a maioria dos corredores (46%) vem da província de Gauteng. Além disso, 3.735 atletas buscarão a medalha “back-to-back” e 4.271 já possuem o “Green Number”, que é o número permanente para quem completou a prova 10 vezes.

Maratona de Pernambuco abre inscrições

As inscrições para a Maratona Internacional de Pernambuco, que acontecerá nos dias 4 e 5 de setembro de 2027, já estão abertas. A prova, da qual participarei, oferece percursos de 5, 10, 21 e 42 km, além de desafios que combinam distâncias. Foram divulgados os valores e os modelos dos três tipos de kit (Vou Correr, Básico e Premium), além das camisetas de cada distância. Para quem quiser se inscrever, é possível usar o cupom CORRIDANOAR para garantir 10% de desconto.

Medalha da Maratona de Nápoles é revelada

Para fechar, a Maratona de Nápoles, na Itália, apresentou sua belíssima medalha. Com um mapa detalhado da cidade e da costa, a peça é um item de colecionador. A prova é organizada por Carlo Capalbo, cidadão napolitano que também está por trás do renomado circuito RunCzech, em Praga, o que garante um alto padrão de qualidade para o evento.
